title: Sommelier Practice: Temperature, Opening, Decanting and Service
quiz.0.question: A guest orders a 2010 Barolo (it is now 2026, 16 years on). How should it be served?
quiz.0.options.0: Pour it at once into a wide decanter and aerate for 2 hours to open the closed tannins
quiz.0.options.1: Pour gently in front of a candle to remove the sediment, and drink straight after, without long aeration
quiz.0.options.2: Open it and pour straight into glasses — an old wine needs no handling
quiz.0.options.3: Chill it in an ice bucket to 10°C so the low temperature keeps the delicate aromas
quiz.0.explanation: A 16-year-old Barolo is an aged wine with plenty of sediment, which needs to be removed by pouring gently in front of a light. Old wines are very fragile and unsuited to long aeration (oxidation makes the wine fall apart and lose its layers). The serving temperature should be around 18°C, not chilled.
quiz.1.question: In summer a guest orders a Chianti Classico with grilled food, and the restaurant is about 28°C. What is the correct serving temperature?
quiz.1.options.0: Serve it at room temperature (28°C), since "serve at room temperature" is the rule
quiz.1.options.1: Chill it for about 15 minutes so it reaches 16-18°C before serving
quiz.1.options.2: Put it in iced water in an ice bucket to cool it quickly to 8°C
quiz.1.options.3: Chill it only after the guest finishes the first glass
quiz.1.explanation: The "room temperature" in "serve at room temperature" means the temperature of a traditional European cellar (about 16-18°C), not 28°C in a Taiwanese summer. In a hot room, Chianti Classico served at 28°C tastes very hot and alcoholic, with loose tannins. The right approach is to chill it to 16-18°C.
quiz.2.question: Which of these Italian wines does NOT need a decanter?
quiz.2.options.0: A young Brunello di Montalcino (2020 vintage)
quiz.2.options.3: A young Amarone della Valpolicella (2019 vintage)
quiz.2.explanation: Prosecco is a sparkling wine, and carbon dioxide is its core appeal. A decanter would make the bubbles dissipate heavily, destroying its main character. Young Brunello and Amarone need aeration to open up, and aged Barolo needs a decanter to remove the sediment — only the sparkling wine clearly rules out a decanter.
quiz.3.question: What is the recommended decanting time for a young Barolo (2020 vintage)?
quiz.3.options.0: 2-3 hours, in a wide decanter for full contact with oxygen, opening the closed, high-tannin structure
quiz.3.options.1: 15 minutes — just a little contact with air is enough
quiz.3.options.2: No decanting needed; open and pour straight into glasses
quiz.3.options.3: 72 hours — young Barolo needs an extremely long decant
quiz.3.explanation: Young Barolo's Nebbiolo, with high tannin + high acidity, is very closed; decant it in a wide decanter for 2-3 hours for full contact with oxygen. This softens the tannins, opens the aromas and integrates the alcohol — too short a time will not work.
slides.0.title: Sommelier Practice: Temperature, Opening, Decanting and Service
slides.0.subtitle: From cellar to table: mastering every key detail that lets Italian wine show at its best
slides.1.title: Serving Temperature: The Invisible Factor in Flavour
slides.1.content:
🫧 Sparkling & white wines

Sparkling: 6-8°C | light whites: 8-10°C | full whites: 10-12°C

Franciacorta/Prosecco → 6-8°C (too cold locks in the aromas; 20 minutes in an ice bucket); Pinot Grigio/Soave/Verdicchio → 8-10°C (leaving room for the fruit); Fiano/Greco di Tufo/Gavi → 10-12°C (warming naturally in the glass helps the minerality unfold)

🍷 Light reds

14-16°C

Bardolino, Schiava, Dolcetto, Lambrusco; in summer they can be lightly chilled (5 minutes in an ice bucket) for extra freshness; these wines taste even fresher and fruitier slightly cool

🍷 Medium reds

16-18°C

Chianti Classico, Barbera d'Asti, Valpolicella; the "room temperature" in "serve at room temperature" means a European cellar's 16-18°C, not 28°C in a Taiwanese summer; chill them in advance in summer

🍷 Powerful aged reds & sweet wines

Powerful reds: 18-20°C | sweet wines: 10-14°C

Barolo/Brunello/Amarone → 18-20°C (above 20°C the alcohol becomes heady and masks delicate aromas); light sweet Moscato → cooler, to keep the fizz; rich sweet Vin Santo/Passito → can be slightly warmer
slides.2.title: The Art of Decanting: Young and Powerful vs Old and Aged
slides.2.content:
Decanting has two quite different purposes: aeration lets a young, closed wine meet oxygen and open its aromas; decanting off sediment keeps the solid sediment of an old wine out of the glass. The two strategies are complete opposites.

🍾 Young, powerful wines: plenty of aeration

  • Young Barolo (under 5 years): high tannin + high acidity, very closed; decant in a wide decanter for 2-3 hours
  • Young Brunello di Montalcino: the tight tannins of Sangiovese Grosso need 1.5-2 hours to show
  • Young Amarone della Valpolicella: the concentrated body made from dried grapes needs to breathe; decant for 1-2 hours to integrate the alcohol
  • Strategy: a wide decanter (the largest contact area) + opening in advance

🕯️ Old wines: gently removing sediment

  • Barolo (10+ years): plenty of sediment; pour slowly in front of a light and stop when sediment reaches the neck
  • Brunello Riserva (15+ years): aged Sangiovese is very fragile; drink straight after removing the sediment, with no further aeration
  • Strategy: stand the bottle upright 24 hours in advance so the sediment sinks; no long aeration after decanting — old wines easily oxidise and fall apart
  • No decanter needed: whites, sparkling wines (the bubbles vanish), light fruity reds (Bardolino/Lambrusco)
slides.3.title: The Logic of Glassware: How Glass Shape Affects Flavour
slides.3.content:
Sparkling glasses

Flute / coupe

Flute: shows the stream of bubbles and keeps the carbon dioxide; suits fresh sparkling wines such as Prosecco

Coupe / standard white-wine glass: shows aromatic complexity better; sommeliers increasingly prefer a wide white-wine glass for top Franciacorta

White-wine glasses

Narrow-rimmed / Burgundy tulip

Narrow-rimmed white glass: keeps acidity fresh; delicate white-flower and mineral aromas are easier to perceive through a narrow rim; suits Pinot Grigio / Soave / Verdicchio

Burgundy tulip: the widest bowl, concentrating delicate aromas; suits aromatically complex whites such as Fiano di Avellino or aged Timorasso

Red-wine glasses

Large Bordeaux / Burgundy

Large Bordeaux (Barolo/Brunello glass): a wide opening maximises contact with oxygen; powerfully tannic wines need this room to "breathe", with aromas gathering at the rim before rising

Burgundy: a wider bowl and narrower rim concentrate delicate floral and fruit aromas; suits aged Nebbiolo, revealing layers of rose and tar
slides.4.title: Four Steps of Restaurant Service: From Understanding Needs to Elegant Opening
slides.4.content:
Step 1: Understand the guest's needs

Food and wine pairing always starts with "people"

Budget range (avoid asking directly; you can say "there are some great choices in this price range"); taste preferences (fuller? lighter? any grapes they dislike?); today's main course (meat/fish/vegetarian?); the occasion (everyday/celebration/business)

Step 2: Plan the wine around the menu

Work back from the main course to build the overall pairing logic

Meat main course → medium to powerful red; fish or seafood → high-acid white; vegetarian → decided by the sauce (tomato-based → red / cream-based → white); several courses → consider a progression from light to rich

Step 3: Offer 3 options

One each at high / medium / low budget

Make sure the guest has room to choose; avoid recommending only the most expensive or only the cheapest; give a short reason for each option (a 10-second elevator pitch); when the guest asks "which is better?", share your own preference rather than dodging

Step 4: Present, open and pour elegantly

The last mile — details create the impression

Present the label facing the guest; cut the foil cleanly; open quietly (a silent opening is preferred); pour a small amount first (about 30 ml) for the host to taste and approve; once approved, serve the guests first and the host last; twist the bottle after each pour to avoid drips
slides.5.title: Key Takeaways
slides.5.points.0: Serving temperatures: sparkling 6-8°C; light whites 8-10°C; full whites 10-12°C; light reds 14-16°C; medium reds 16-18°C; powerful reds 18-20°C
slides.5.points.1: The "room temperature" in "serve at room temperature" is a European cellar's 16-18°C, not 28°C in a Taiwanese summer
slides.5.points.2: Young, powerful wines (Barolo/Brunello/Amarone) need aerating in a wide decanter for 1.5-3 hours to open closed tannins and aromas
slides.5.points.3: Old wines (Barolo/Brunello over 10 years) need gentle decanting off the sediment in front of a light, then drinking straight away — no long aeration
slides.5.points.4: Never decant sparkling wine — the bubbles vanish, destroying its core character
slides.5.points.5: Glass logic: a large Bordeaux glass for powerful reds (the largest contact area); a narrow-rimmed glass for delicate whites; a flute or a wide white-wine glass for sparkling
slides.5.points.6: Four steps of restaurant service: understand needs → plan around the menu → offer 3 options (high/medium/low) → present and open elegantly
slides.5.points.7: The sommelier's first task: serving the guest's experience, not enforcing dogmatic rules

slides.6.questions.4.question: When recommending wine to guests in a restaurant, what is the sommelier's best approach?
slides.6.questions.4.options.0: Recommend only the most expensive wines to ensure top quality
slides.6.questions.4.options.1: Recommend only the cheapest wines so guests won't regret it
slides.6.questions.4.options.2: Offer one option each at high, medium and low budget, with a short reason for each
slides.6.questions.4.options.3: Let guests decide alone — the sommelier should not volunteer suggestions
slides.6.questions.4.explanation: A great sommelier serves the guest's experience rather than enforcing rules. Offering three options at different budgets gives the guest room to choose, with a 10-second "elevator pitch" for each option's character. When the guest asks "which is better?", the sommelier should share a personal preference rather than dodge.
